Description

Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).[1]

Adversaries may connect to a remote system over RDP/RDS to expand access if the service is enabled and allows access to accounts with known credentials. Adversaries will likely use Credential Access techniques to acquire credentials to use with RDP. Adversaries may also use RDP in conjunction with the Accessibility Features or Terminal Services DLL for Persistence.[2]

Detection

DET0327 — Multi-event Detection Strategy for RDP-Based Remote Logins and Post-Access Activity

AN0931 — Analytic 0931 (Platforms: Windows)

Remote Desktop (RDP) logon by a user followed by unusual process execution, file access, or lateral movement activity within a short timeframe.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4624, 4648 (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4778, EventCode=4779 (DC0088 Logon Session Metadata)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=3, 22 (DC0082 Network Connection Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • TimeWindow — Temporal threshold to correlate login with post-login activity (e.g., 5 minutes)
  • UserContext — Tune for non-admin users or service accounts expected to use RDP
  • ProcessList — Define suspicious post-login processes such as cmd.exe, powershell.exe, certutil.exe
  • HostAccessPatterns — Scope detection to uncommon or first-time access between source and destination hosts

Mitigations

  • M1018 — User Account ManagementLimit remote user permissions if remote access is necessary.
  • M1026 — Privileged Account ManagementConsider removing the local Administrators group from the list of groups allowed to log in through RDP.
  • M1028 — Operating System ConfigurationChange GPOs to define shorter timeouts sessions and maximum amount of time any single session can be active. Change GPOs to specify the maximum amount of time that a disconnected session stays active on the RD session host server.[3]
  • M1030 — Network SegmentationDo not leave RDP accessible from the internet. Enable firewall rules to block RDP traffic between network security zones within a network.
  • M1032 — Multi-factor AuthenticationUse multi-factor authentication for remote logins.[4]
  • M1035 — Limit Access to Resource Over NetworkUse remote desktop gateways.
  • M1042 — Disable or Remove Feature or ProgramDisable the RDP service if it is unnecessary.
  • M1047 — AuditAudit the Remote Desktop Users group membership regularly. Remove unnecessary accounts and groups from Remote Desktop Users groups.

Description

Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

SMB is a file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol for Windows machines on the same network or domain. Adversaries may use SMB to interact with file shares, allowing them to move laterally throughout a network. Linux and macOS implementations of SMB typically use Samba.

Windows systems have hidden network shares that are accessible only to administrators and provide the ability for remote file copy and other administrative functions. Example network shares include C$, ADMIN$, and IPC$. Adversaries may use this technique in conjunction with administrator-level Valid Accounts to remotely access a networked system over SMB,[1] to interact with systems using remote procedure calls (RPCs),[2] transfer files, and run transferred binaries through remote Execution. Example execution techniques that rely on authenticated sessions over SMB/RPC are Scheduled Task/Job, Service Execution, and Windows Management Instrumentation. Adversaries can also use NTLM hashes to access administrator shares on systems with Pass the Hash and certain configuration and patch levels.[3]

Detection

DET0530 — Multi-Event Detection for SMB Admin Share Lateral Movement

AN1468 — Analytic 1468 (Platforms: Windows)

An SMB-based remote file share access followed by lateral movement actions such as remote service creation, task scheduling, or suspicious process execution on the target host using ADMIN$ or C$ shares.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4624, 4648 (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=3, 22 (DC0082 Network Connection Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • ShareName — Targeted admin share path, such as C$, ADMIN$, IPC$
  • TimeWindow — Correlation window between remote file access and remote execution (e.g., 5-10 minutes)
  • UserContext — Distinguish expected remote administrators vs. rare/first-time access by specific users
  • ProcessList — List of suspicious binaries or tools executed post remote copy (e.g., cmd.exe, powershell.exe, runonce.exe)

Mitigations

  • M1026 — Privileged Account ManagementDeny remote use of local admin credentials to log into systems. Do not allow domain user accounts to be in the local Administrators group multiple systems.
  • M1027 — Password PoliciesDo not reuse local administrator account passwords across systems. Ensure password complexity and uniqueness such that the passwords cannot be cracked or guessed.
  • M1035 — Limit Access to Resource Over NetworkConsider disabling Windows administrative shares.
  • M1037 — Filter Network TrafficConsider using the host firewall to restrict file sharing communications such as SMB. [4]

  • S1242 — Qilin (Malware): Qilin can embed a copy of PsExec within its payload and place it in the %Temp% directory under a randomly generated filename.[72][73]
  • S1212 — RansomHub (Malware): RansomHub can use credentials provided in its configuration to move laterally from the infected machine over SMBv2.[74]
  • S0019 — Regin (Malware): The Regin malware platform can use Windows admin shares to move laterally.[75]
  • S1073 — Royal (Malware): Royal can use SMB to connect to move laterally.[76]
  • S0446 — Ryuk (Malware): Ryuk has used the C$ network share for lateral movement.[77]
  • S0140 — Shamoon (Malware): Shamoon accesses network share(s), enables share access to the target device, copies an executable payload to the target system, and uses a Scheduled Task/Job to execute the malware.[78]
  • S0603 — Stuxnet (Malware): Stuxnet propagates to available network shares.[79]
  • S0672 — Zox (Malware): Zox has the ability to use SMB for communication.[80]
  • S1187 — reGeorg (Malware): reGeorg has the ability to tunnel SMB sessions.[81]
  • S0350 — zwShell (Malware): zwShell has been copied over network shares to move laterally.[82]
  • S1063 — Brute Ratel C4 (Tool): Brute Ratel C4 has the ability to use SMB to pivot in compromised networks.[83][84][85]
  • S0039 — Net (Tool): Lateral movement can be done with Net through net use commands to connect to the on remote systems.[86]

testcase: Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
details:
ATT&CK ID

T1021.003

Matrix

Enterprise ATT&CK v19.1

Tactic(s)

Lateral Movement

Platform(s)

Windows

Technique version

1.3

Parent technique

T1021 — Remote Services

Reference

https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/003

Description

Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

The Windows Component Object Model (COM) is a component of the native Windows application programming interface (API) that enables interaction between software objects, or executable code that implements one or more interfaces. Through COM, a client object can call methods of server objects, which are typically Dynamic Link Libraries (DLL) or executables (EXE). Distributed COM (DCOM) is transparent middleware that extends the functionality of COM beyond a local computer using remote procedure call (RPC) technology.[1][2]

Permissions to interact with local and remote server COM objects are specified by access control lists (ACL) in the Registry.[3] By default, only Administrators may remotely activate and launch COM objects through DCOM.[4]

Through DCOM, adversaries operating in the context of an appropriately privileged user can remotely obtain arbitrary and even direct shellcode execution through Office applications[5] as well as other Windows objects that contain insecure methods.[6][7] DCOM can also execute macros in existing documents[8] and may also invoke Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) execution directly through a COM created instance of a Microsoft Office application[9], bypassing the need for a malicious document. DCOM can be used as a method of remotely interacting with Windows Management Instrumentation. [10]

Detection

DET0285 — Multi-Event Behavioral Detection for DCOM-Based Remote Code Execution

AN0791 — Analytic 0791 (Platforms: Windows)

A remote DCOM invocation by a privileged account using RPC (port 135), followed by abnormal process instantiation or module loading on the remote system indicative of code execution.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4624, 4648 (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=3, 22 (DC0082 Network Connection Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=7 (DC0016 Module Load)

Tuning considerations:

  • TimeWindow — Correlate RPC activity with remote process creation within a configurable time window (e.g., 300s)
  • UserContext — Identify rare or first-time DCOM invocations by specific accounts
  • ProcessName — List of suspicious executables commonly abused via DCOM (e.g., excel.exe, wmiprvse.exe)
  • RemoteHostList — Known set of systems that should or should not be invoking DCOM activity

Mitigations

  • M1026 — Privileged Account ManagementModify Registry settings (directly or using Dcomcnfg.exe) in HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Classes\AppID\{{AppID_GUID}} associated with the process-wide security of individual COM applications.[3] · Modify Registry settings (directly or using Dcomcnfg.exe) in HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Ole associated with system-wide security defaults for all COM applications that do not set their own process-wide security.[11] [4]
  • M1030 — Network SegmentationEnable Windows firewall, which prevents DCOM instantiation by default.
  • M1042 — Disable or Remove Feature or ProgramConsider disabling DCOM through Dcomcnfg.exe.[12]
  • M1048 — Application Isolation and SandboxingEnsure all COM alerts and Protected View are enabled.[13]

Procedure Examples

  • S0154 — Cobalt Strike (Malware): Cobalt Strike can deliver Beacon payloads for lateral movement by leveraging remote COM execution.[14]
  • S0363 — Empire (Tool): Empire can utilize Invoke-DCOM to leverage remote COM execution for lateral movement.[15]
  • S0692 — SILENTTRINITY (Tool): SILENTTRINITY can use System namespace methods to execute lateral movement using DCOM.[16]

ATT&CK ID

T1021.004

Matrix

Enterprise ATT&CK v19.1

Tactic(s)

Lateral Movement

Platform(s)

ESXi, Linux, macOS

Technique version

1.3

Parent technique

T1021 — Remote Services

Reference

https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/004

Description

Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

SSH is a protocol that allows authorized users to open remote shells on other computers. Many Linux and macOS versions come with SSH installed by default, although typically disabled until the user enables it. On ESXi, SSH can be enabled either directly on the host (e.g., via vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh) or via vCenter.[1][2][3] The SSH server can be configured to use standard password authentication or public-private keypairs in lieu of or in addition to a password. In this authentication scenario, the user’s public key must be in a special file on the computer running the server that lists which keypairs are allowed to login as that user (i.e., SSH Authorized Keys).

Detection

DET0596 — Behavioral Detection of Remote SSH Logins Followed by Post-Login Execution

AN1638 — Analytic 1638 (Platforms: Linux)

SSH login from a remote system (via sshd), followed by user context execution of suspicious binaries or privilege escalation behavior.

Log sources:

  • auditd:EXECVE — EXECVE (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • linux:syslog — None (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • NSM:Flow — TCP port 22 traffic (DC0078 Network Traffic Flow)

Tuning considerations:

  • TimeWindow — Defines correlation window from login to first post-SSH process (e.g., 60s)
  • SuspiciousProcessList — List of binaries considered unusual in SSH context (e.g., nc, base64, bash -i)
  • UsernameFilter — Accounts of interest for SSH logins (e.g., root, admin)

AN1639 — Analytic 1639 (Platforms: macOS)

SSH login detected via Unified Logs, followed by unusual process execution, especially outside normal user behavior patterns.

Log sources:

  • macos:unifiedlog — process = 'sshd' (DC0088 Logon Session Metadata)
  • macos:unifiedlog — process = 'ssh' OR eventMessage CONTAINS 'ssh' (DC0085 Network Traffic Content)
  • macos:osquery — process_events (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • TimeWindow — Time range to correlate post-SSH activities (e.g., 45s)
  • UserContext — Define authorized users to reduce false positives
  • CommandLineKeywords — Suspicious terms like reverse shells, base64, curl

AN1640 — Analytic 1640 (Platforms: ESXi)

SSH login via hostd or /var/log/auth.log, followed by CLI access to host shell or file manipulation in restricted areas.

Log sources:

  • esxi:auth — None (DC0088 Logon Session Metadata)
  • esxi:shell — None (DC0064 Command Execution)
  • esxi:vmkernel — port 22 access (DC0078 Network Traffic Flow)

Tuning considerations:

  • AllowedUsers — Legitimate SSH users to this host
  • TimeWindow — Correlate SSH login and unauthorized commands or shell access
  • CommandList — Flag commands like esxcli, rm, chmod post-login

Mitigations

  • M1018 — User Account ManagementLimit which user accounts are allowed to login via SSH.
  • M1032 — Multi-factor AuthenticationRequire multi-factor authentication for SSH connections wherever possible, such as password protected SSH keys.
  • M1042 — Disable or Remove Feature or ProgramDisable the SSH daemon on systems that do not require it, especially ESXi servers. For macOS, ensure Remote Login is disabled under Sharing Preferences.[4]

Procedure Examples

  • C0032 — C0032 (Campaign): During the C0032 campaign, TEMP.Veles relied on encrypted SSH-based tunnels to transfer tools and for remote command/program execution.[5]
  • C0029 — Cutting Edge (Campaign): During Cutting Edge, threat actors used SSH for lateral movement.[6]
  • C0049 — Leviathan Australian Intrusions (Campaign): Leviathan used SSH brute force techniques to move laterally within victim environments during Leviathan Australian Intrusions.[7]
  • G0087 — APT39 (Group): APT39 used secure shell (SSH) to move laterally among their targets.[8]
  • G1023 — APT5 (Group): APT5 has used SSH for lateral movement in compromised environments including for enabling access to ESXi host servers.[9]
  • G0143 — Aquatic Panda (Group): Aquatic Panda used SSH with captured user credentials to move laterally in victim environments.[10]
  • G0098 — BlackTech (Group): BlackTech has used Putty for remote access.[11]
  • G1016 — FIN13 (Group): FIN13 has remotely accessed compromised environments via secure shell (SSH) for lateral movement.[12]
  • G0046 — FIN7 (Group): FIN7 has used SSH to move laterally through victim environments.[13]
  • G0117 — Fox Kitten (Group): Fox Kitten has used the PuTTY and Plink tools for lateral movement.[14]
  • G0036 — GCMAN (Group): GCMAN uses Putty for lateral movement.[15]
  • G0119 — Indrik Spider (Group): Indrik Spider has used SSH for lateral movement.[16]
  • G0032 — Lazarus Group (Group): Lazarus Group used SSH and the PuTTy PSCP utility to gain access to a restricted segment of a compromised network.[17]
  • G0065 — Leviathan (Group): Leviathan used ssh for internal reconnaissance.[18]
  • G0049 — OilRig (Group): OilRig has used Putty to access compromised systems.[19]
  • G0106 — Rocke (Group): Rocke has spread its coinminer via SSH.[20]
  • G1045 — Salt Typhoon (Group): Salt Typhoon has modified the loopback address on compromised switches and used them as the source of SSH connections to additional devices within the target environment, allowing them to bypass access control lists (ACLs).[21]

ATT&CK ID

T1021.005

Matrix

Enterprise ATT&CK v19.1

Tactic(s)

Lateral Movement

Platform(s)

Linux, Windows, macOS

Technique version

1.2

Parent technique

T1021 — Remote Services

Reference

https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/005

Description

Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC). VNC is a platform-independent desktop sharing system that uses the RFB (“remote framebuffer”) protocol to enable users to remotely control another computer’s display by relaying the screen, mouse, and keyboard inputs over the network.[1]

VNC differs from Remote Desktop Protocol as VNC is screen-sharing software rather than resource-sharing software. By default, VNC uses the system's authentication, but it can be configured to use credentials specific to VNC.[2][3]

Adversaries may abuse VNC to perform malicious actions as the logged-on user such as opening documents, downloading files, and running arbitrary commands. An adversary could use VNC to remotely control and monitor a system to collect data and information to pivot to other systems within the network. Specific VNC libraries/implementations have also been susceptible to brute force attacks and memory usage exploitation.[4][5][6][7][8][9]

Detection

DET0178 — Behavioral Detection of Unauthorized VNC Remote Control Sessions

AN0504 — Analytic 0504 (Platforms: Windows)

Detection of VNC service or executable starting unexpectedly, followed by user session creation and interactive desktop activity (mouse/keyboard simulation).

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4624, 4648 (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • NSM:Flow — port 5900 inbound (DC0078 Network Traffic Flow)

Tuning considerations:

  • TimeWindow — Correlate VNC process with user logon activity within defined time span
  • VNCBinaryList — Trackable VNC executable names (e.g., vncserver.exe, winvnc.exe)
  • LogonType — Limit detection to interactive logons (type 10)

AN0505 — Analytic 0505 (Platforms: Linux)

Spawning of VNC-related processes (e.g., x11vnc, vncserver) coupled with authentication logs and port listening behavior on TCP 5900.

Log sources:

  • auditd:EXECVE — None (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • linux:syslog — None (DC0088 Logon Session Metadata)
  • NSM:Flow — TCP port 5900 open (DC0078 Network Traffic Flow)

Tuning considerations:

  • ListeningPort — Default VNC port (5900) but may vary in config
  • ProcessNameFilter — Filter specific VNC binaries in process execution logs
  • UserContext — Scope detection to non-service or high-privilege accounts

AN0506 — Analytic 0506 (Platforms: macOS)

Detection of VNC-based remote control via screensharingd activity in Unified Logs along with concurrent remote login activity or suspicious user interaction.

Log sources:

  • macos:unifiedlog — authentication (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • macos:osquery — process_events (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • NSM:firewall — inbound connection to port 5900 (DC0078 Network Traffic Flow)

Tuning considerations:

  • AuthenticationPredicate — Unified log predicate to refine suspicious screensharing access
  • TimeWindow — Time between VNC connection and follow-on activity (e.g., 30s)
  • UserActivitySpike — Mouse/keyboard interaction spike immediately post-VNC login

Mitigations

  • M1033 — Limit Software InstallationRestrict software installation to user groups that require it. A VNC server must be manually installed by the user or adversary.
  • M1037 — Filter Network TrafficVNC defaults to TCP ports 5900 for the server, 5800 for browser access, and 5500 for a viewer in listening mode. Filtering or blocking these ports will inhibit VNC traffic utilizing default ports.
  • M1042 — Disable or Remove Feature or ProgramUninstall any VNC server software where not required.
  • M1047 — AuditInventory workstations for unauthorized VNC server software.

Procedure Examples

  • G0046 — FIN7 (Group): FIN7 has used TightVNC to control compromised hosts.[10]
  • G0117 — Fox Kitten (Group): Fox Kitten has installed TightVNC server and client on compromised servers and endpoints for lateral movement.[11]
  • G0036 — GCMAN (Group): GCMAN uses VNC for lateral movement.[12]
  • G0047 — Gamaredon Group (Group): Gamaredon Group has used VNC tools, including UltraVNC, to remotely interact with compromised hosts.[13][14][15]
  • S0484 — Carberp (Malware): Carberp can start a remote VNC session by downloading a new plugin.[16]
  • S1014 — DanBot (Malware): DanBot can use VNC for remote access to targeted systems.[17]
  • S1160 — Latrodectus (Malware): Latrodectus has routed C2 traffic using Keyhole VNC.[18]
  • S0279 — Proton (Malware): Proton uses VNC to connect into systems.[19]
  • S0266 — TrickBot (Malware): TrickBot has used a VNC module to monitor the victim and collect information to pivot to valuable systems on the network [20][21]
  • S0670 — WarzoneRAT (Malware): WarzoneRAT has the ability of performing remote desktop access via a VNC console.[22]
  • S0412 — ZxShell (Malware): ZxShell supports functionality for VNC sessions.[23]

Description

Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

WinRM is the name of both a Windows service and a protocol that allows a user to interact with a remote system (e.g., run an executable, modify the Registry, modify services).[1] It may be called with the winrm command or by any number of programs such as PowerShell.[2] WinRM can be used as a method of remotely interacting with Windows Management Instrumentation.[3]

Detection

DET0477 — Behavioral Detection of WinRM-Based Remote Access

AN1313 — Analytic 1313 (Platforms: Windows)

Adversaries using WinRM to remotely execute commands, launch child processes, or access WMI. The detection chain includes service use, network activity, remote session logon, and process creation within a short temporal window.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4624, 4648 (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • WinEventLog:WinRM — EventCode=6 (DC0041 Service Metadata)
  • NSM:Connections — Inbound on ports 5985/5986 (DC0078 Network Traffic Flow)

Tuning considerations:

  • TimeWindow — Defines max time between remote shell creation and child process execution (e.g., 60 seconds)
  • UserContext — Scope to unexpected remote user logons (non-admins, service accounts)
  • CommandLineAnomalyScore — Score for suspicious command usage via WinRM (e.g., encoded PowerShell)
  • KnownAdminHosts — List of trusted systems allowed to use WinRM legitimately

Mitigations

  • M1026 — Privileged Account ManagementIf the service is necessary, lock down critical enclaves with separate WinRM accounts and permissions.
  • M1030 — Network SegmentationIf the service is necessary, lock down critical enclaves with separate WinRM infrastructure and follow WinRM best practices on use of host firewalls to restrict WinRM access to allow communication only to/from specific devices.[4]
  • M1042 — Disable or Remove Feature or ProgramDisable the WinRM service.

Procedure Examples

  • C0048 — Operation MidnightEclipse (Campaign): During Operation MidnightEclipse, threat actors used WinRM to move laterally in targeted networks.[5]
  • C0024 — SolarWinds Compromise (Campaign): During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used WinRM via PowerShell to execute commands and payloads on remote hosts.[6]
  • G0114 — Chimera (Group): Chimera has used WinRM for lateral movement.[7]
  • G1016 — FIN13 (Group): FIN13 has leveraged WMI to move laterally within a compromised network via application servers and SQL servers.[8]
  • G1053 — Storm-0501 (Group): Storm-0501 has utilized the post-exploitation tool known as Evil-WinRM that uses PowerShell over Windows Remote Management (WinRM) for remote code execution.[9]
  • G0027 — Threat Group-3390 (Group): Threat Group-3390 has used WinRM to enable remote execution.[10]
  • G0102 — Wizard Spider (Group): Wizard Spider has used Window Remote Management to move laterally through a victim network.[11]
  • S0154 — Cobalt Strike (Malware): Cobalt Strike can use WinRM to execute a payload on a remote host.[12][13]
  • S1063 — Brute Ratel C4 (Tool): Brute Ratel C4 can use WinRM for pivoting.[14]
  • S0692 — SILENTTRINITY (Tool): SILENTTRINITY tracks TrustedHosts and can move laterally to these targets via WinRM.[15]

Reference

Description

Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using Valid Accounts that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities. The adversary may then perform management actions or access cloud-hosted resources as the logged-on user.

Many enterprises federate centrally managed user identities to cloud services, allowing users to login with their domain credentials in order to access the cloud control plane. Similarly, adversaries may connect to available cloud services through the web console or through the cloud command line interface (CLI) (e.g., Cloud API), using commands such as Connect-AZAccount for Azure PowerShell, Connect-MgGraph for Microsoft Graph PowerShell, and gcloud auth login for the Google Cloud CLI.

In some cases, adversaries may be able to authenticate to these services via Application Access Token instead of a username and password.

Detection

DET0008 — Behavioral Detection of Remote Cloud Logins via Valid Accounts

AN0017 — Analytic 0017 (Platforms: IaaS)

Cloud login from atypical geolocation or user-agent string, followed by resource enumeration or infrastructure manipulation using cloud CLI/API

Log sources:

  • AWS:CloudTrail — ConsoleLogin, AssumeRole, ListResources (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • gcp:audit — None (DC0064 Command Execution)

Tuning considerations:

  • IPGeoRiskScore — Tunable scoring system for evaluating geo-divergent or TOR-origin logins
  • UserAgentFingerprint — Flag rare CLI tools or browser-based sessions
  • SessionDuration — Threshold for how long between login and API access
  • CloudResourceScope — Limit monitoring to high-value resource groups or sensitive tenants

AN0018 — Analytic 0018 (Platforms: Identity Provider)

Federated login using SSO or OAuth grant to cloud control plane, followed by directory or permissions enumeration

Log sources:

  • Okta:SystemLog — user.authentication.sso, app.oauth.grant (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • SSOApplicationScope — Tune based on applications federated to high-priv cloud assets
  • ClientIDScope — Filter based on expected OIDC clients used for login
  • LoginVelocity — Track multiple geographic logins within short windows

AN0019 — Analytic 0019 (Platforms: Office Suite)

Login to M365 or Google Workspace from CLI tools or unexpected source IPs, followed by mailbox or document access

Log sources:

  • m365:unified — FileAccessed, MailboxAccessed (DC0055 File Access)
  • m365:unified — UserLoggedIn (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • DevicePlatformMismatch — Raise alerts on login from CLI when user typically uses web-only
  • SensitiveDocumentAccessPattern — Track access to documents labeled as internal/confidential
  • AccessFrequencyThreshold — Tune for high-volume document reads post login

AN0020 — Analytic 0020 (Platforms: SaaS)

Remote access to third-party SaaS with OAuth or API tokens post-initial compromise, followed by sensitive data access or configuration changes

Log sources:

  • saas:auth — LoginSuccess, APIKeyUse, AdminAction (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • OAuthTokenAge — Older tokens issued before password change may indicate compromise
  • AppScope — Restrict detection to high-value or regulated SaaS apps

Mitigations

  • M1026 — Privileged Account ManagementLimit the number of high-privileged domain and cloud accounts, and ensure that these are not used for day-to-day operations. Ensure that on-premises accounts do not have privileged cloud permissions and that isolated, cloud-only accounts are used for managing cloud environments.[1]
  • M1032 — Multi-factor AuthenticationUse multi-factor authentication on cloud services whenever possible.

Procedure Examples

  • C0027 — C0027 (Campaign): During C0027, Scattered Spider used compromised Azure credentials for credential theft activity and lateral movement to on-premises systems.[2]
  • G0016 — APT29 (Group): APT29 has leveraged compromised high-privileged on-premises accounts synced to Office 365 to move laterally into a cloud environment, including through the use of Azure AD PowerShell.[3]
  • G1015 — Scattered Spider (Group): Scattered Spider has also leveraged pre-existing AWS EC2 instances for lateral movement and data collection purposes.[4]
  • G1053 — Storm-0501 (Group): Storm-0501 has used compromised Entra Connect Sync Server to move laterally within the victim environment.[5]

Reference

Description

Adversaries may leverage Valid Accounts to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods. Many cloud providers offer interactive connections to virtual infrastructure that can be accessed through the Cloud API, such as Azure Serial Console[1], AWS EC2 Instance Connect[2][3], and AWS System Manager.[4].

Methods of authentication for these connections can include passwords, application access tokens, or SSH keys. These cloud native methods may, by default, allow for privileged access on the host with SYSTEM or root level access.

Adversaries may utilize these cloud native methods to directly access virtual infrastructure and pivot through an environment.[5] These connections typically provide direct console access to the VM rather than the execution of scripts (i.e., Cloud Administration Command).

Detection

DET0211 — Detection of Direct VM Console Access via Cloud-Native Methods

AN0594 — Analytic 0594 (Platforms: IaaS)

Direct login to cloud-hosted virtual machines via cloud-native access methods (e.g., EC2 Instance Connect, Azure Serial Console, SSM), followed by command execution or privilege escalation on the VM

Log sources:

  • AWS:CloudTrail — SendSSHPublicKey, StartSession (SSM), EC2InstanceConnect (DC0067 Logon Session Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • TimeWindow — Correlates cloud login to host activity within a reasonable time span (e.g., < 60 seconds)
  • CloudAuthMethod — Filters based on access vector: SSH key, SSM session, or Console connect
  • SessionOriginRegion — Identifies sessions from out-of-region or untrusted networks
  • TargetInstanceTags — Filters sensitive systems or production assets for alert tuning

Mitigations

  • M1018 — User Account ManagementLimit which users are allowed to access compute infrastructure via cloud native methods.
  • M1042 — Disable or Remove Feature or ProgramIf direct virtual machine connections are not required for administrative use, disable these connection types where feasible.

Description

Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest. Sensitive data can be collected from any removable media (optical disk drive, USB memory, etc.) connected to the compromised system prior to Exfiltration. Interactive command shells may be in use, and common functionality within cmd may be used to gather information.

Some adversaries may also use Automated Collection on removable media.

Detection

DET0511 — Detection of Data Access and Collection from Removable Media

AN1410 — Analytic 1410 (Platforms: Windows)

Adversary mounts a USB device and begins enumerating, copying, or compressing files using scripting engines, cmd, or remote access tools.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4663, 4670, 4656 (DC0055 File Access)
  • WinEventLog:System — EventCode=2003 (DC0042 Drive Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • VolumeLabel — Can tune based on known removable device labels or whitelist
  • TimeWindow — Controls timing between device mount and sensitive file access
  • TargetFileType — Tune for sensitive file extensions (e.g., .docx, .pdf, .csv)

AN1411 — Analytic 1411 (Platforms: Linux)

Adversary mounts external drive to /media or /mnt then accesses or copies targeted data via shell, cp, or tar.

Log sources:

  • auditd:SYSCALL — open, read, mount (DC0055 File Access)
  • journald:systemd — udisks2 or udevd logs (DC0042 Drive Creation)
  • auditd:SYSCALL — execve (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • MountPathRegex — Filter for unexpected or user-defined mount locations (e.g., /media/usb*)
  • AccessMask — Tune based on read/write access types seen during collection

AN1412 — Analytic 1412 (Platforms: macOS)

Adversary attaches USB drive and accesses sensitive files using Finder, cp, or bash scripts.

Log sources:

  • macos:unifiedlog — log stream --predicate 'eventMessage contains "USBMSC"' (DC0042 Drive Creation)
  • fs:fsusage — file reads/writes from /Volumes/ (DC0055 File Access)
  • macos:osquery — process_events (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • VolumePath — Tune by filtering removable media mounted under /Volumes
  • UserContext — Correlate activity to admin or service accounts for priority

Mitigations

  • M1057 — Data Loss PreventionData loss prevention can restrict access to sensitive data and detect sensitive data that is unencrypted.

Description

Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit. This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses.

Payloads may be compressed, archived, or encrypted in order to avoid detection. These payloads may be used during Initial Access or later to mitigate detection. Sometimes a user's action may be required to open and Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information for User Execution. The user may also be required to input a password to open a password protected compressed/encrypted file that was provided by the adversary.[1] Adversaries may also use compressed or archived scripts, such as JavaScript.

Portions of files can also be encoded to hide the plain-text strings that would otherwise help defenders with discovery.[2] Payloads may also be split into separate, seemingly benign files that only reveal malicious functionality when reassembled.[3]

Adversaries may also abuse Command Obfuscation to obscure commands executed from payloads or directly via Command and Scripting Interpreter. Environment variables, aliases, characters, and other platform/language specific semantics can be used to evade signature based detections and application control mechanisms.[4][5][6]

Detection

DET0378 — Behavioral Detection of Obfuscated Files or Information

AN1064 — Analytic 1064 (Platforms: Windows)

Correlates script execution or suspicious parent processes with creation or modification of encoded, compressed, or encrypted file formats (e.g., .zip, .7z, .enc) and abnormal command-line syntax or PowerShell obfuscation.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4688 (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=11 (DC0039 File Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • PayloadEntropyThreshold — Tune entropy threshold to distinguish obfuscation from legitimate compression
  • TimeWindow — Adjust correlation window between script execution and encoded file creation
  • SuspiciousParentProcessList — Customize based on environment to include LOLBins or admin tools misused for obfuscation

AN1065 — Analytic 1065 (Platforms: Linux)

Detects use of gzip, base64, tar, or openssl in scripts or commands that encode/encrypt files after file staging or system enumeration.

Log sources:

  • auditd:SYSCALL — execve (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • auditd:SYSCALL — open, write (DC0061 File Modification)
  • linux:cli — Shell history logs (DC0064 Command Execution)

Tuning considerations:

  • CommandRegex — Customize for tools seen in environment (e.g., gzip, bzip2, xz)
  • SensitivePathList — Specify file paths likely targeted for obfuscation (e.g., /etc/, /home/)

AN1066 — Analytic 1066 (Platforms: macOS)

Monitors use of archive or encryption tools (zip, openssl) tied to user-scripted activity or binaries writing encoded payloads under /Users or /Volumes.

Log sources:

  • macos:unifiedlog — log stream --predicate 'processImagePath contains "zip" OR "base64"' (DC0064 Command Execution)
  • macos:osquery — file_events (DC0039 File Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • FilenameExtensionList — Tunable to identify uncommon or encrypted file formats (e.g., .enc, .b64, .xz)
  • UserContext — Tune to prioritize unexpected file access by service accounts

AN1067 — Analytic 1067 (Platforms: Network Devices)

Identifies transfer of base64, uuencoded, or high-entropy files over HTTP, FTP, or custom protocols in lateral movement or exfiltration streams.

Log sources:

  • networkdevice:IDS — content inspection / PCAP / HTTP body (DC0085 Network Traffic Content)

Tuning considerations:

  • EntropyThreshold — Adjust threshold to reduce false positives in compressed but benign data
  • ProtocolScope — Refine by enabling inspection of specific exfil vectors (e.g., FTP, HTTP POST)

AN1068 — Analytic 1068 (Platforms: ESXi)

Detects encoded PowerCLI or Base64-encoded payloads staged via datastore uploads or shell access (e.g., ESXi Shell or backdoored VIBs).

Log sources:

  • esxi:vmkernel — Datastore modification events (DC0059 File Metadata)
  • esxi:hostd — Remote access API calls and file uploads (DC0021 OS API Execution)

Tuning considerations:

  • StagingLocation — Tune based on observed adversary paths (e.g., /vmfs/volumes/...)
  • EncodedLengthThreshold — Tune length of encoded payloads before triggering detection

Mitigations

  • M1017 — User TrainingEnsure that a finite amount of ingress points to a software deployment system exist with restricted access for those required to allow and enable newly deployed software.
  • M1040 — Behavior Prevention on EndpointOn Windows 10+, enable Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules to prevent execution of potentially obfuscated payloads. [7]
  • M1047 — AuditConsider periodic review of common fileless storage locations (such as the Registry or WMI repository) to potentially identify abnormal and malicious data.
  • M1049 — Antivirus/AntimalwareAnti-virus can be used to automatically detect and quarantine suspicious files. Consider utilizing the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) on Windows 10+ to analyze commands after being processed/interpreted. [8]

  • S0512 — FatDuke (Malware): FatDuke can use base64 encoding, string stacking, and opaque predicates for obfuscation.[108]
  • S0182 — FinFisher (Malware): FinFisher is heavily obfuscated in many ways, including through the use of spaghetti code in its functions in an effort to confuse disassembly programs. It also uses a custom XOR algorithm to obfuscate code.[109][110]
  • S0355 — Final1stspy (Malware): Final1stspy obfuscates strings with base64 encoding.[111]
  • S0696 — Flagpro (Malware): Flagpro has been delivered within ZIP or RAR password-protected archived files.[112]
  • S9033 — Fooder (Malware): Fooder has stored its embedded payload in encrypted form within the binary, using a hardcoded key modified at runtime to produce the AES decryption key.[113]
  • S1138 — Gootloader (Malware): The Gootloader first stage script is obfuscated using random alpha numeric strings.[114][115]
  • S0690 — Green Lambert (Malware): Green Lambert has encrypted strings.[116][117]
  • S0632 — GrimAgent (Malware): GrimAgent has used Rotate on Right (RoR) and Rotate on Left (RoL) functionality to encrypt strings.[118]
  • S0132 — H1N1 (Malware): H1N1 uses multiple techniques to obfuscate strings, including XOR.[119]
  • S0070 — HTTPBrowser (Malware): HTTPBrowser's code may be obfuscated through structured exception handling and return-oriented programming.[120]
  • S9007 — HTTPTroy (Malware): HTTPTroy has obfuscated strings using Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) instructions to hinder analysis and detection.[32]
  • S0499 — Hancitor (Malware): Hancitor has used Base64 to encode malicious links.[121]
  • S0203 — Hydraq (Malware): Hydraq uses basic obfuscation in the form of spaghetti code.[122][123]
  • S0189 — ISMInjector (Malware): ISMInjector is obfuscated with the off-the-shelf SmartAssembly .NET obfuscator created by red-gate.com.[124]
  • S0604 — Industroyer (Malware): Industroyer uses heavily obfuscated code in its Windows Notepad backdoor.[9]
  • S0259 — InnaputRAT (Malware): InnaputRAT uses an 8-byte XOR key to obfuscate API names and other strings contained in the payload.[125]
  • S0260 — InvisiMole (Malware): InvisiMole avoids analysis by encrypting all strings, internal files, configuration data and by using a custom executable format.[126][127]
  • S0201 — JPIN (Malware): A JPIN uses a encrypted and compressed payload that is disguised as a bitmap within the resource section of the installer.[128]
  • S0265 — Kazuar (Malware): Kazuar is obfuscated using the open source ConfuserEx protector. Kazuar also obfuscates the name of created files/folders/mutexes and encrypts debug messages written to log files using the Rijndael cipher.[129]
  • S0607 — KillDisk (Malware): KillDisk uses VMProtect to make reverse engineering the malware more difficult.[130]
  • S0641 — Kobalos (Malware): Kobalos encrypts all strings using RC4 and bundles all functionality into a single function call.[131]
  • S9020 — LODEINFO (Malware): LODEINFO has used control flow flattening to obfuscate code.[132]
  • S0681 — Lizar (Malware): Lizar has obfuscated the fingerprint of the victim system, the local IP address, and the Fowler-Noll-V 1 (FNV-1) hash of the local IP address using an XOR operation. The data is then sent to the C2 server.[133]
  • S0447 — Lokibot (Malware): Lokibot has obfuscated strings with base64 encoding.[134]
  • S1213 — Lumma Stealer (Malware): Lumma Stealer has used SmartAssembly to obfuscate .NET payloads.[135]
  • S0167 — Matryoshka (Malware): Matryoshka obfuscates API function names using a substitute cipher combined with Base64 encoding.[136]
  • S0449 — Maze (Malware): Maze has decrypted strings and other important information during the encryption process. Maze also calls certain functions dynamically to hinder analysis.[137]
  • S0051 — MiniDuke (Malware): MiniDuke can use control flow flattening to obscure code.[108]
  • S0198 — NETWIRE (Malware): NETWIRE has used a custom obfuscation algorithm to hide strings including Registry keys, APIs, and DLL names.[138]
  • S0353 — NOKKI (Malware): NOKKI uses Base64 encoding for strings.[139]
  • S9025 — NOOPLDR (Malware): NOOPLDR can use control flow flattening to help hide malicious code.[140][141]
  • S0336 — NanoCore (Malware): NanoCore’s plugins were obfuscated with Eazfuscater.NET 3.3.[142]
  • S1090 — NightClub (Malware): NightClub can obfuscate strings using the congruential generator (LCG): staten+1 = (690069 × staten + 1) mod 232.[143]
  • S0138 — OLDBAIT (Malware): OLDBAIT obfuscates internal strings and unpacks them at startup.[78]
  • S0264 — OopsIE (Malware): OopsIE uses the Confuser protector to obfuscate an embedded .Net Framework assembly used for C2. OopsIE also encodes collected data in hexadecimal format before writing to files on disk and obfuscates strings.[144][145]
  • S0229 — Orz (Malware): Some Orz strings are base64 encoded, such as the embedded DLL known as MockDll.[146]
  • S0598 — P.A.S. Webshell (Malware): P.A.S. Webshell can use encryption and base64 encoding to hide strings and to enforce access control once deployed.[147]
  • S0150 — POSHSPY (Malware): POSHSPY appends a file signature header (randomly selected from six file types) to encrypted data prior to upload or download.[148]
  • S1228 — PUBLOAD (Malware): PUBLOAD has obfuscated DLL names using the ror13AddHash32 algorithm.[35]
  • S0196 — PUNCHBUGGY (Malware): PUNCHBUGGY has hashed most its code's functions and encrypted payloads with base64 and XOR.[149]
  • S0197 — PUNCHTRACK (Malware): PUNCHTRACK is loaded and executed by a highly obfuscated launcher.[150]
  • S0517 — Pillowmint (Malware): Pillowmint has obfuscated the AES key used for encryption.[151]
  • S0124 — Pisloader (Malware): Pisloader obfuscates files by splitting strings into smaller sub-strings and including "garbage" strings that are never used. The malware also uses return-oriented programming (ROP) technique and single-byte XOR to obfuscate data.[152]
  • S0013 — PlugX (Malware): PlugX can use API hashing and modify the names of strings to evade detection.[82][41]
  • S0428 — PoetRAT (Malware): PoetRAT has used a custom encryption scheme for communication between scripts.[153]
  • S0012 — PoisonIvy (Malware): PoisonIvy hides any strings related to its own indicators of compromise.[154]
  • S0518 — PolyglotDuke (Malware): PolyglotDuke can custom encrypt strings.[108]
  • S0393 — PowerStallion (Malware): PowerStallion uses a XOR cipher to encrypt command output written to its OneDrive C2 server.[155]
  • S0650 — QakBot (Malware): QakBot has hidden code within Excel spreadsheets by turning the font color to white and splitting it across multiple cells.[156]
  • S0240 — ROKRAT (Malware): ROKRAT can encrypt data prior to exfiltration by using an RSA public key.[19][157]
  • S0148 — RTM (Malware): RTM strings, network data, configuration, and modules are encrypted with a modified RC4 algorithm.[158][159]
  • S0458 — Ramsay (Malware): Ramsay has base64-encoded its portable executable and hidden itself under a JPG header. Ramsay can also embed information within document footers.[160]
  • S1130 — Raspberry Robin (Malware): Raspberry Robin uses mixed-case letters for filenames and commands to evade detection.[161]
  • S0511 — RegDuke (Malware): RegDuke can use control-flow flattening or the commercially available .NET Reactor for obfuscation.[108]
  • S9037 — RustyWater (Malware): RustyWater has an obfuscated function (i.e. love_me__()) that dynamically reconstructs the string WScript.Shell using hard-coded ASCII values and the Chr() function.[162]
  • S0446 — Ryuk (Malware): Ryuk can use anti-disassembly and code transformation obfuscation techniques.[92]
  • S0461 — SDBbot (Malware): SDBbot has the ability to XOR the strings for its installer component with a hardcoded 128 byte key.[163]
  • S0063 — SHOTPUT (Malware): SHOTPUT is obscured using XOR encoding and appended to a valid GIF file.[164][165]
  • S1104 — SLOWPULSE (Malware): SLOWPULSE can hide malicious code in the padding regions between legitimate functions in the Pulse Secure libdsplibs.so file.[166]
  • S0559 — SUNBURST (Malware): SUNBURST obfuscated collected system information using a FNV-1a + XOR algorithm.[167]
  • S0562 — SUNSPOT (Malware): SUNSPOT encrypted log entries it collected with the stream cipher RC4 using a hard-coded key. It also uses AES128-CBC encrypted blobs for SUNBURST source code and data extracted from the SolarWinds Orion <MsBuild.exe` process.[168]
  • S1064 — SVCReady (Malware): SVCReady can encrypt victim data with an RC4 cipher.[169]
  • S1018 — Saint Bot (Malware): Saint Bot has been obfuscated to help avoid detection.[170]
  • S1099 — Samurai (Malware): Samurai can encrypt the names of requested APIs.[171]
  • S1085 — Sardonic (Malware): Sardonic can use certain ConfuserEx features for obfuscation and can be encoded in a base64 string.[172]
  • S0596 — ShadowPad (Malware): ShadowPad has encrypted its payload, a virtual file system, and various files.[173][23]
  • S9008 — Shai-Hulud (Malware): Shai-Hulud has utilized double-base64 encoding to store stolen secrets within the Github Action Logs within the victim account.[174][175][176][177] Shai-Hulud has also leveraged three layers of base64 encoding of exfiltrated data for anti-forensic purposes.[178]
  • S0140 — Shamoon (Malware): Shamoon contains base64-encoded strings.[179]
  • S0623 — Siloscape (Malware): Siloscape itself is obfuscated and uses obfuscated API calls.[180]
  • S1035 — Small Sieve (Malware): Small Sieve has the ability to use a custom hex byte swapping encoding scheme combined with an obfuscated Base64 function to protect program strings and Telegram credentials.[181]
  • S1086 — Snip3 (Malware): Snip3 has the ability to obfuscate strings using XOR encryption.[182]
  • S0627 — SodaMaster (Malware): SodaMaster can use "stackstrings" for obfuscation.[106]
  • S0615 — SombRAT (Malware): SombRAT can encrypt strings with XOR-based routines and use a custom AES storage format for plugins, configuration, C2 domains, and harvested data.[183][184][185]
  • S0516 — SoreFang (Malware): SoreFang has the ability to encode and RC6 encrypt data sent to C2.[186]
  • S0142 — StreamEx (Malware): StreamEx obfuscates some commands by using statically programmed fragments of strings when starting a DLL. It also uses a one-byte xor against 0x91 to encode configuration data.[187]
  • S1183 — StrelaStealer (Malware): StrelaStealer has been distributed in ISO archives.[188] StrelaStealer has been delivered in encrypted, password-protected ZIP archives.[189]
  • S0242 — SynAck (Malware): SynAck payloads are obfuscated prior to compilation to inhibit analysis and/or reverse engineering.[190][191]
  • S0560 — TEARDROP (Malware): TEARDROP created and read from a file with a fake JPG header, and its payload was encrypted with a simple rotating XOR cipher.[167][192][193]
  • S0467 — TajMahal (Malware): TajMahal has used an encrypted Virtual File System to store plugins.[194]
  • S0266 — TrickBot (Malware): TrickBot uses non-descriptive names to hide functionality.[195]
  • S0094 — Trojan.Karagany (Malware): Trojan.Karagany can base64 encode and AES-128-CBC encrypt data prior to transmission.[196]
  • S0647 — Turian (Malware): Turian can use VMProtect for obfuscation.[21]
  • S0476 — Valak (Malware): Valak has the ability to base64 encode and XOR encrypt strings.[197][198][199]
  • S0117 — XTunnel (Malware): A version of XTunnel introduced in July 2015 obfuscated the binary using opaque predicates and other techniques in a likely attempt to obfuscate it and bypass security products.[200]
  • S0283 — jRAT (Malware): jRAT’s Java payload is encrypted with AES.[201] Additionally, backdoor files are encrypted using DES as a stream cipher. Later variants of jRAT also incorporated AV evasion methods such as Java bytecode obfuscation via the commercial Allatori obfuscation tool.[202]
  • S1063 — Brute Ratel C4 (Tool): Brute Ratel C4 has used encrypted payload files and maintains an encrypted configuration structure in memory.[203][204]
  • S0465 — CARROTBALL (Tool): CARROTBALL has used a custom base64 alphabet to decode files.[205]
  • S0434 — Imminent Monitor (Tool): Imminent Monitor has encrypted the spearphish attachments to avoid detection from email gateways; the debugger also encrypts information before sending to the C2.[14]
  • S0500 — MCMD (Tool): MCMD can Base64 encode output strings prior to sending to C2.[206]
  • S0594 — Out1 (Tool): Out1 has the ability to encode data.[207]
  • S0332 — Remcos (Tool): Remcos uses RC4 and base64 to obfuscate data, including Registry entries and file paths.[208] Remcos can also employ control flow flattening to hinder analysis.[209]
  • S0445 — ShimRatReporter (Tool): ShimRatReporter encrypted gathered information with a combination of shifting and XOR using a static key.[210]
  • S0633 — Sliver (Tool): Sliver obfuscates configuration and other static files using native Go libraries such as garble and gobfuscate to inhibit configuration analysis and static detection.[211]

testcase: Obfuscated Files or Information: Binary Padding
details:
ATT&CK ID

T1027.001

Matrix

Enterprise ATT&CK v19.1

Tactic(s)

Stealth

Platform(s)

Linux, macOS, Windows

Technique version

2.0

Parent technique

T1027 — Obfuscated Files or Information

Reference

https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/001

Description

Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware. This can be done without affecting the functionality or behavior of a binary, but can increase the size of the binary beyond what some security tools are capable of handling due to file size limitations.

Binary padding effectively changes the checksum of the file and can also be used to avoid hash-based blocklists and static anti-virus signatures.[1] The padding used is commonly generated by a function to create junk data and then appended to the end or applied to sections of malware.[2] Increasing the file size may decrease the effectiveness of certain tools and detection capabilities that are not designed or configured to scan large files. This may also reduce the likelihood of being collected for analysis. Public file scanning services, such as VirusTotal, limits the maximum size of an uploaded file to be analyzed.[3]

Detection

DET0553 — Detection Strategy for Obfuscated Files or Information: Binary Padding

AN1528 — Analytic 1528 (Platforms: Windows)

Detects the creation or execution of padded binary files (e.g., large size but minimal legitimate content) followed by process execution or lateral movement from the host.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4688 (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4663, 4670, 4656 (DC0055 File Access)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=11 (DC0039 File Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • FileSizeThresholdMB — Threshold size in MB to determine suspicious padding
  • TimeWindow — Correlation time window between file creation and execution
  • UserContext — Scope the detection to suspicious or non-standard user accounts

AN1529 — Analytic 1529 (Platforms: Linux)

Detects abnormal creation of binary files with significant size that are subsequently executed or accessed by non-standard users.

Log sources:

  • auditd:SYSCALL — open (DC0055 File Access)
  • auditd:SYSCALL — execve (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • linux:osquery — file_events (DC0039 File Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • FileSizeThresholdMB — Defines how large a file must be to consider it padded
  • UserContext — Target abnormal user behavior outside of expected automation
  • TimeWindow — Time window for correlating file creation and execution

AN1530 — Analytic 1530 (Platforms: macOS)

Monitors for anomalous binary files written to disk with padded size and subsequent execution by user or service context.

Log sources:

  • macos:unifiedlog — process:spawn (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • fs:fsusage — file write (DC0039 File Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • FileSizeThresholdMB — Padded binary threshold for file size
  • TimeWindow — Detection correlation window for execution after file creation
  • UserContext — Filters for specific users or groups such as admin or service accounts

Procedure Examples

  • G0016 — APT29 (Group): APT29 used large size files to avoid detection by security solutions with hardcoded size limits.[4]
  • G1024 — Akira (Group): Akira has used binary padding to obfuscate payloads.[5]
  • G0060 — BRONZE BUTLER (Group): BRONZE BUTLER downloader code has included "0" characters at the end of the file to inflate the file size in a likely attempt to evade anti-virus detection.[6][7]
  • G0126 — Higaisa (Group): Higaisa performed padding with null bytes before calculating its hash.[8]
  • G0094 — Kimsuky (Group): Kimsuky has performed padding of PowerShell command line code with over 100 spaces.[9]
  • G0065 — Leviathan (Group): Leviathan has inserted garbage characters into code, presumably to avoid anti-virus detection.[10]
  • G0002 — Moafee (Group): Moafee has been known to employ binary padding.[11]
  • G0040 — Patchwork (Group): Patchwork apparently altered NDiskMonitor samples by adding four bytes of random letters in a likely attempt to change the file hashes.[12]
  • S0268 — Bisonal (Malware): Bisonal has appended random binary data to the end of itself to generate a large binary.[13]
  • S1070 — Black Basta (Malware): Black Basta had added data prior to the Portable Executable (PE) header to prevent automatic scanners from identifying the payload.[14]
  • S1149 — CHIMNEYSWEEP (Malware): The CHIMNEYSWEEP installer has been padded with null bytes to inflate its size.[15]
  • S9016 — Caminho (Malware): Caminho can use junk code for obfuscation.[16]
  • S0244 — Comnie (Malware): Comnie appends a total of 64MB of garbage data to a file to deter any security products in place that may be scanning files on disk.[17]
  • S0614 — CostaBricks (Malware): CostaBricks has added the entire unobfuscated code of the legitimate open source application Blink to its code.[18]
  • S0082 — Emissary (Malware): A variant of Emissary appends junk data to the end of its DLL file to create a large file that may exceed the maximum size that anti-virus programs can scan.[19]
  • S0367 — Emotet (Malware): Emotet inflates malicious files and malware as an evasion technique.[20]
  • S0477 — Goopy (Malware): Goopy has had null characters padded in its malicious DLL payload.[21]
  • S0531 — Grandoreiro (Malware): Grandoreiro has added BMP images to the resources section of its Portable Executable (PE) file increasing each binary to at least 300MB in size.[22]
  • S0632 — GrimAgent (Malware): GrimAgent has the ability to add bytes to change the file hash.[23]
  • S9018 — HeartCrypt (Malware): HeartCrypt can add several hundred thousand kilobytes of null padding to payloads before saving onto the file system.[24]
  • S0528 — Javali (Malware): Javali can use large obfuscated libraries to hinder detection and analysis.[25]
  • S0236 — Kwampirs (Malware): Before writing to disk, Kwampirs inserts a randomly generated string into the middle of the decrypted payload in an attempt to evade hash-based detections.[26]
  • S1160 — Latrodectus (Malware): Latrodectus has been obfuscated with a 129 byte sequence of junk data prepended to the file.[27]
  • S1185 — LightSpy (Malware): LightSpy's configuration file is appended to the end of the binary. For example, the last 0x1d0 bytes of one sample is an AES encrypted configuration file with a static key of 3e2717e8b3873b29.[28]
  • S0013 — PlugX (Malware): PlugX has utilized junk code and opaque predicates in payloads to hinder analysis.[29]

testcase: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
details:
ATT&CK ID

T1027.002

Matrix

Enterprise ATT&CK v19.1

Tactic(s)

Stealth

Platform(s)

Linux, macOS, Windows

Technique version

2.0

Parent technique

T1027 — Obfuscated Files or Information

Reference

https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/002

Description

Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code. Software packing is a method of compressing or encrypting an executable. Packing an executable changes the file signature in an attempt to avoid signature-based detection. Most decompression techniques decompress the executable code in memory. Virtual machine software protection translates an executable's original code into a special format that only a special virtual machine can run. A virtual machine is then called to run this code.[1]

Utilities used to perform software packing are called packers. Example packers are MPRESS and UPX. A more comprehensive list of known packers is available, but adversaries may create their own packing techniques that do not leave the same artifacts as well-known packers to evade defenses.[2]

Detection

DET0023 — Obfuscated Binary Unpacking Detection via Behavioral Patterns

AN0066 — Analytic 0066 (Platforms: Windows)

Detection of unpacking behavior through abnormal memory allocation, followed by executable code injection and execution from non-image sections.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=10 (DC0035 Process Access)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • ParentProcessName — To scope detections to suspicious parent-child process relationships typical of loaders or droppers.
  • AllocationSizeThreshold — To tune for unusually large virtual memory allocations that might indicate unpacked payloads.

AN0067 — Analytic 0067 (Platforms: Linux)

Correlates ELF file execution with high-entropy writable memory segments and self-modifying code patterns.

Log sources:

  • auditd:SYSCALL — execve (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • auditd:SYSCALL — mprotect (DC0020 Process Modification)

Tuning considerations:

  • EntropyThreshold — Useful for tuning unpacked sections containing high entropy indicative of compression or encryption.
  • TimeWindow — Can be tuned to correlate file writes to execution within a set timeframe.

AN0068 — Analytic 0068 (Platforms: macOS)

Detection of packed Mach-O binaries unpacking into memory and transferring control to dynamically modified code segments.

Log sources:

  • macos:unifiedlog — process::exec (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • macos:endpointsecurity — ES_EVENT_MMAP (DC0020 Process Modification)

Tuning considerations:

  • SignedBinaryContext — Helps to distinguish between signed/unsigned packed binaries (common in legitimate vs. malicious cases).
  • UserContext — Can be used to scope to specific users or service accounts targeted in attacks.

Mitigations

  • M1049 — Antivirus/AntimalwareEmploy heuristic-based malware detection. Ensure updated virus definitions and create custom signatures for observed malware.

Matrix

Enterprise ATT&CK v19.1

Tactic(s)

Stealth

Platform(s)

Linux, macOS, Windows

Technique version

2.0

Parent technique

T1027 — Obfuscated Files or Information

Reference

https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003

Description

Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital media such as images, audio tracks, video clips, or text files.

Duqu was an early example of malware that used steganography. It encrypted the gathered information from a victim's system and hid it within an image before exfiltrating the image to a C2 server.[1]

By the end of 2017, a threat group used Invoke-PSImage to hide PowerShell commands in an image file (.png) and execute the code on a victim's system. In this particular case the PowerShell code downloaded another obfuscated script to gather intelligence from the victim's machine and communicate it back to the adversary.[2]

Detection

DET0119 — Detection Strategy for Steganographic Abuse in File & Script Execution

AN0331 — Analytic 0331 (Platforms: Windows)

Detects execution of image viewers or PowerShell scripts accessing or decoding files with mismatched MIME headers or embedded script-like byte patterns; often correlated with suspicious parent-child process lineage and outbound connections.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=3, 22 (DC0082 Network Connection Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Security — EventCode=4663, 4670, 4656 (DC0055 File Access)

Tuning considerations:

  • ParentProcessImage — Tune to identify image editors/viewers invoking script interpreters (e.g., mspaint.exe > powershell.exe)
  • MimeHeaderMismatchTolerance — Adjust tolerance for image file headers that do not match file extensions or content structure
  • TimeWindow — Define the temporal range to correlate decoding → execution → network beaconing

AN0332 — Analytic 0332 (Platforms: Linux)

Detects access to media files followed by execution of scripts (bash, Python, etc.) referencing those same files, or outbound traffic triggered shortly after file read. Correlates unusual use of tools like steghide, exiftool, or image libraries.

Log sources:

  • auditd:SYSCALL — open (DC0055 File Access)
  • auditd:SYSCALL — execve (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • auditd:SYSCALL — connect (DC0082 Network Connection Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • MonitoredToolsList — Define the list of steganographic or image-parsing tools to alert on (e.g., steghide, imagemagick)
  • ScriptInterpreterMatch — Tune to detect script engines accessing media files (e.g., python script.py image.png)

AN0333 — Analytic 0333 (Platforms: macOS)

Detects manipulation of PNG, JPG, or GIF files by user-initiated scripts followed by script execution or exfiltration behavior, especially from osascript, python, or bash, in combination with LaunchAgent persistence or curl activity.

Log sources:

  • macos:osquery — file_events (DC0055 File Access)
  • macos:osquery — process_events (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • macos:unifiedlog — network connection events (DC0082 Network Connection Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • StegoToolNamePatterns — Adapt to known or emerging tools using stego methods on macOS (e.g., Invoke-PSImage, stegsolve)
  • ParentScriptSources — Update list of trusted versus unknown scripting hosts launching activity tied to image handling

Procedure Examples

  • C0023 — Operation Ghost (Campaign): During Operation Ghost, APT29 used steganography to hide payloads inside valid images.[3]
  • C0005 — Operation Spalax (Campaign): For Operation Spalax, the threat actors used packers that read pixel data from images contained in PE files' resource sections and build the next layer of execution from the data.[4]
  • G0099 — APT-C-36 (Group): APT-C-36 has used steganography to hide malicious code, typically in the resource section of executable files.[5][6][6][7]
  • G0067 — APT37 (Group): APT37 uses steganography to send images to users that are embedded with shellcode.[8][9]
  • G0138 — Andariel (Group): Andariel has hidden malicious executables within PNG files.[10][11]
  • G0060 — BRONZE BUTLER (Group): BRONZE BUTLER has used steganography in multiple operations to conceal malicious payloads.[12]
  • G1006 — Earth Lusca (Group): Earth Lusca has used steganography to hide shellcode in a BMP image file.[13]
  • G0065 — Leviathan (Group): Leviathan has used steganography to hide stolen data inside other files stored on Github.[14]
  • G0069 — MuddyWater (Group): MuddyWater has stored obfuscated JavaScript code in an image file named temp.jpg.[15]
  • G0127 — TA551 (Group): TA551 has hidden encoded data for malware DLLs in a PNG.[16]
  • G0081 — Tropic Trooper (Group): Tropic Trooper has used JPG files with encrypted payloads to mask their backdoor routines and evade detection.[17]
  • S0469 — ABK (Malware): ABK can extract a malicious Portable Executable (PE) from a photo.[12]
  • S0473 — Avenger (Malware): Avenger can extract backdoor malware from downloaded images.[12]
  • S0470 — BBK (Malware): BBK can extract a malicious Portable Executable (PE) from a photo.[12]
  • S0234 — Bandook (Malware): Bandook has used .PNG images within a zip file to build the executable. [18]
  • S0659 — Diavol (Malware): Diavol has obfuscated its main code routines within bitmap images as part of its anti-analysis techniques.[19]
  • S0483 — IcedID (Malware): IcedID has embedded binaries within RC4 encrypted .png files.[20]
  • S0513 — LiteDuke (Malware): LiteDuke has used image files to hide its loader component.[3]
  • S0644 — ObliqueRAT (Malware): ObliqueRAT can hide its payload in BMP images hosted on compromised websites.[21]
  • S0439 — Okrum (Malware): Okrum's payload is encrypted and embedded within its loader, or within a legitimate PNG file.[22]
  • S1145 — Pikabot (Malware): Pikabot loads a set of PNG images stored in the malware's resources section (RCDATA), each with an encrypted section containing portions of the core Pikabot core module. These sections are loaded and decrypted using a bitwise XOR operation with a hardcoded 32 bit key.[23]
  • S0518 — PolyglotDuke (Malware): PolyglotDuke can use steganography to hide C2 information in images.[3]
  • S0139 — PowerDuke (Malware): PowerDuke uses steganography to hide backdoors in PNG files, which are also encrypted using the Tiny Encryption Algorithm (TEA).[24]
  • S0654 — ProLock (Malware): ProLock can use .jpg and .bmp files to store its payload.[25]
  • S0495 — RDAT (Malware): RDAT can also embed data within a BMP image prior to exfiltration.[26]
  • S0565 — Raindrop (Malware): Raindrop used steganography to locate the start of its encoded payload within legitimate 7-Zip code.[27]
  • S0458 — Ramsay (Malware): Ramsay has PE data embedded within JPEG files contained within Word documents.[28]
  • S0511 — RegDuke (Malware): RegDuke can hide data in images, including use of the Least Significant Bit (LSB).[3]
  • S0471 — build_downer (Malware): build_downer can extract malware from a downloaded JPEG.[12]
  • S0231 — Invoke-PSImage (Tool): Invoke-PSImage can be used to embed a PowerShell script within the pixels of a PNG file.[29]

testcase: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery
details:
ATT&CK ID

T1027.004

Matrix

Enterprise ATT&CK v19.1

Tactic(s)

Stealth

Platform(s)

Linux, macOS, Windows

Technique version

2.0

Parent technique

T1027 — Obfuscated Files or Information

Reference

https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/004

Description

Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe[1], csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.[2]

Source code payloads may also be encrypted, encoded, and/or embedded within other files, such as those delivered as a Phishing. Payloads may also be delivered in formats unrecognizable and inherently benign to the native OS (ex: EXEs on macOS/Linux) before later being (re)compiled into a proper executable binary with a bundled compiler and execution framework.[3]

Detection

DET0501 — Detection Strategy for Compile After Delivery - Source Code to Executable Transformation

AN1381 — Analytic 1381 (Platforms: Windows)

Detects compilation activity using csc.exe, ilasm.exe, or msbuild.exe initiated by user-space processes outside typical development environments, followed by execution or network activity from newly written binaries.

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=11 (DC0039 File Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=3, 22 (DC0082 Network Connection Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • ParentProcessName — Filter for unexpected users (non-dev) launching compilers like csc.exe or msbuild.exe
  • OutputDirectoryPath — Adjust paths for sensitive file write zones (e.g., C:\Users\Public\, %TEMP%, or Desktop)
  • TimeWindow — Tune the correlation window between compilation and subsequent execution or C2

AN1382 — Analytic 1382 (Platforms: Linux)

Detects GCC or Clang invoked on suspicious file paths (e.g., /tmp/, ~/Downloads) with output to executable binaries, followed by execution or outbound traffic from these binaries.

Log sources:

  • auditd:SYSCALL — execve (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • auditd:SYSCALL — open,create (DC0039 File Creation)
  • NSM:Flow — conn.log (DC0082 Network Connection Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • CompilerBinaryPath — Specify path and binaries for detection (e.g., /usr/bin/gcc, /opt/mingw/bin/gcc)
  • FilePermissionProfile — Match uncommon chmod behavior post-compilation (e.g., +x in /tmp or home directories)

AN1383 — Analytic 1383 (Platforms: macOS)

Detects non-standard compilation activity via Xcode CLI tools or bundled GCC/MONO packages writing new executable files and executing them outside dev environments (e.g., user Downloads folder).

Log sources:

  • macos:unifiedlog — process activity, exec events (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • macos:osquery — file_events (DC0039 File Creation)

testcase: Obfuscated Files or Information: Indicator Removal from Tools
details:
ATT&CK ID

T1027.005

Matrix

Enterprise ATT&CK v19.1

Tactic(s)

Stealth

Platform(s)

Linux, macOS, Windows

Technique version

2.0

Parent technique

T1027 — Obfuscated Files or Information

Reference

https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/005

Description

Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed. They can modify the tool by removing the indicator and using the updated version that is no longer detected by the target's defensive systems or subsequent targets that may use similar systems.

A good example of this is when malware is detected with a file signature and quarantined by anti-virus software. An adversary who can determine that the malware was quarantined because of its file signature may modify the file to explicitly avoid that signature, and then re-use the malware.

Detection

DET0189 — Detection Strategy for Indicator Removal from Tools - Post-AV Evasion Modification

AN0540 — Analytic 0540 (Platforms: Windows)

Detection of known tools or malware flagged by antivirus, followed by a near-term drop of a similar binary with modified signature and resumed activity (execution, C2, or persistence).

Log sources:

  • WinEventLog:Application — EventCode=1000 (DC0038 Application Log Content)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=1 (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • WinEventLog:Sysmon — EventCode=11 (DC0039 File Creation)

Tuning considerations:

  • AVAlertMessage — Vendor-specific signature string or detection message that can be correlated to threat intel context.
  • TimeWindow — The time between AV alert and similar file/process activity (e.g., 5–30 minutes)
  • FilenameSimilarityThreshold — String or hash similarity thresholds between original and modified binary.

AN0541 — Analytic 0541 (Platforms: Linux)

Detection of anti-malware quarantining or flagging a tool, followed by a new binary written to disk with a similar function or name and a resumed process chain.

Log sources:

  • auditd:SYSCALL — execve (DC0032 Process Creation)
  • auditd:SYSCALL — open, rename (DC0020 Process Modification)
  • linux:osquery — file_events (DC0059 File Metadata)
  • EDR:detection — ThreatDetected, QuarantineLog (DC0038 Application Log Content)

Tuning considerations:

  • PathWatchlist — Tunable list of directories often abused for dropped binaries (e.g., /tmp, ~/.cache, /opt/soft/).
  • ProcessAncestryDepth — Limit how far up the tree to trace tool modification behavior for detection.

AN0542 — Analytic 0542 (Platforms: macOS)

Detection of XProtect or AV quarantining a known tool, followed by modification (file size, hash, string) and subsequent re-execution by the same or related user.

Log sources:

  • macos:unifiedlog — quarantine or AV-related subsystem (DC0038 Application Log Content)
  • macos:osquery — file_events (DC0059 File Metadata)

Tuning considerations:

  • BinaryChangeThreshold — File hash delta or binary string diff score to tolerate renamed/mutated variants.
  • UserContext — User or group expected to use dev tools; reduce false positives from legitimate repacking.

Procedure Examples

  • C0014 — Operation Wocao (Campaign): During Operation Wocao, threat actors edited variable names within the Impacket suite to avoid automated detection.[1]
  • C0030 — Triton Safety Instrumented System Attack (Campaign): In the Triton Safety Instrumented System Attack, TEMP.Veles modified files based on the open-source project cryptcat in an apparent attempt to decrease anti-virus detection rates.[2]
  • G0022 — APT3 (Group): APT3 has been known to remove indicators of compromise from tools.[3]
  • G0009 — Deep Panda (Group): Deep Panda has updated and modified its malware, resulting in different hash values that evade detection.[4]
  • G0093 — GALLIUM (Group): GALLIUM ensured each payload had a unique hash, including by using different types of packers.[5]
  • G0049 — OilRig (Group): OilRig has tested malware samples to determine AV detection and subsequently modified the samples to ensure AV evasion.[6][7]
  • G0040 — Patchwork (Group): Patchwork apparently altered NDiskMonitor samples by adding four bytes of random letters in a likely attempt to change the file hashes.[8]
  • G0010 — Turla (Group): Based on comparison of Gazer versions, Turla made an effort to obfuscate strings in the malware that could be used as IoCs, including the mutex name and named pipe.[9]
  • G1048 — UNC3886 (Group): UNC3886 has replaced atomic indicators mentioned in threat intelligence publications, sometimes as quickly as under a week after release.[10]
  • S0154 — Cobalt Strike (Malware): Cobalt Strike includes a capability to modify the Beacon payload to eliminate known signatures or unpacking methods.[11][12]
  • S0187 — Daserf (Malware): Analysis of Daserf has shown that it regularly undergoes technical improvements to evade anti-virus detection.[13]
  • S0237 — GravityRAT (Malware): The author of GravityRAT submitted samples to VirusTotal for testing, showing that the author modified the code to try to hide the DDE object in a different part of the document.[14]
  • S0260 — InvisiMole (Malware): InvisiMole has undergone regular technical improvements in an attempt to evade detection.[15]
  • S0587 — Penquin (Malware): Penquin can remove strings from binaries.[16]
  • S0650 — QakBot (Malware): QakBot can make small changes to itself in order to change its checksum and hash value.[17][18]
  • S0559 — SUNBURST (Malware): SUNBURST source code used generic variable names and pre-obfuscated strings, and was likely sanitized of developer comments before being added to SUNSPOT.[19]
  • S0579 — Waterbear (Malware): Waterbear can scramble functions not to be executed again with random values.[20]
  • S0194 — PowerSploit (Tool): PowerSploit's Find-AVSignature AntivirusBypass module can be used to locate single byte anti-virus signatures.[21][22]
